title: Partition Expansion
explain: Systems that scale by moving data fix the number of partitions at bootstrap, far more than the number of nodes, and give each node several. Adding a node hands it a few whole partitions, so no key is re-hashed. The hard ceiling is the partition count, which is why I pick it with headroom up front.
model:
Keys map to partitions by a stable hash; only the **partition to node assignment** changes when you scale.

```
before:  A: P1 P4 P7 P10    B: P2 P5 P8 P11    C: P3 P6 P9 P12
add D :  A: P1 P7 P10       B: P2 P8 P11       C: P3 P9 P12      D: P4 P5 P6
```

Only 3 of 12 partitions move and the new node pulls them in parallel. (The user's note shows the same shape with 10 partitions: D takes P4, P5, P6 and P10.)

Versus `hash(key) mod nodes`: changing the node count remaps almost every key (4 to 5 nodes moves 80 percent).

**The hard limit is the partition count.** A partition is the smallest unit you can move. With 50 partitions and 50 nodes, a 51st node owns nothing. Raising the number of partitions means splitting or re-hashing data, a heavy migration that systems usually do not automate.

Sizing: well above the largest node count you expect, with many divisors (512 for 8 growing to 40 nodes), but not so high that per-partition overhead (metadata, files, replication streams) bites. Moving the data is [rebalancing](#/sd/f/rebalance); filling a new partition from history is [backfill](#/sd/f/backfill). Related: [hash buckets](#/sd/f/hash-bucketing), [partitioning](#/sd/f/partitioning), [token rebalancing](#/sd/f/token-rebalancing).

details.q: 12 partitions on 3 nodes, 4 each. You add a fourth node and want an even spread. How many partitions move?
details.a: Three: the target is 3 per node, so each old node gives up one partition, and nothing else moves.

details.q: 50 partitions on 50 nodes and you add 25 more nodes. What happens?
details.a: The new nodes sit idle. A partition is the unit of assignment, so at most 50 nodes can own data. To use them you must raise the partition count, which is a heavy split or re-hash.

details.q: Why do fixed partitions beat `hash(key) mod nodes` when growing?
details.a: A key's partition never changes; only whole partitions move between nodes. With mod N, changing N remaps most keys, so nearly all data moves.

details.q: The cluster is 8 nodes now and will be about 40 in three years. What initial partition count?
details.a: Something like 512: far above 40 so each node still owns several, divisible in many ways for even spreads, and small enough that per-partition overhead stays low. 8 or 40 gives no headroom; millions of partitions waste overhead.

details.q: How does a node actually take over a partition?
details.a: The new node joins owning nothing, a coordinator picks a few partitions from each old node, each is copied while the old owner keeps serving, routing switches when it is caught up, and the old owner deletes its copy. See [rebalance](#/sd/f/rebalance).

details.q: What do you do when you really need more partitions?
details.a: Split partitions or re-hash into a larger number, usually as a planned, manual migration (a [backfill](#/sd/f/backfill) with cutover). Some systems support dynamic splitting of hot or large partitions, but it is not free.

prompts.q: Explain fixed-partition scaling and why it beats mod-N hashing.
points: Partition count fixed at bootstrap, many per node
Key to partition mapping never changes
Adding a node moves a few whole partitions
Mod N remaps almost all keys when N changes

prompts.q: Walk through adding a node to a fixed-partition cluster.
points: Coordinator picks partitions from existing nodes
Copy while old owner serves, then switch routing
Move the minimum, throttle the copy

prompts.q: When is adding nodes not enough, and how do you choose the initial partition count?
points: Node count reaches partition count, or partitions get too big or hot
Need to split or re-hash, a heavy migration
Pick well above the max node count with many divisors
Not so high that per-partition overhead dominates
